title: Play, distraction and preparing children for procedures
blurb: Use therapeutic play, honest preparation and age-matched distraction to reduce fear and pain during procedures.
question: A 6-year-old needs a cannula this afternoon and is frightened of needles. He asks the nurse, 'Will it hurt?' How should the nurse prepare him and support him during the procedure?

teach.body: Play is how children make sense of the world. In hospital, therapeutic play helps children feel safe and in control, express feelings and cope with fear, pain and anxiety. Health play specialists, registered with the Hospital Play Staff Education Trust (HPSET), use play for preparation, distraction and debrief. Plain English: a prepared, distracted child copes better, and the procedure goes better too.
teach.cite: NICE NG204 1.6.2; OUH Children's Play in Hospital leaflet (2024)

teach.h: Preparing a child for a procedure (NG204 1.6.2)
items: Give honest information about what will happen, in words and play suited to the child's age.
Be honest about possible pain and what will be done to ease it.
Use therapeutic play and distraction; create a calm environment before, during and after.
Offer choices the child can genuinely make (whose lap, which distraction), not whether the procedure happens if it is needed.
Believe the child's pain afterwards; never say a painful procedure 'didn't really hurt'.

teach.caption: The technique depends on the child's age, stage, needs, wishes and the procedure.
NG204 1.8.3: separate treatment areas from those for play and recreation.

teach.body: Telling a child 'it won't hurt' when it might teaches them not to trust you next time. Say it may feel like a sharp scratch or pinch for a moment, explain what will help (numbing cream, a hand to hold, a game), and give them a job, such as holding very still or blowing bubbles. Uphold their experience afterwards.

items: Noah, 6, needs a cannula. Nurse Bea applies topical anaesthetic cream and asks the play specialist to see him beforehand.
With a medical play doll and a real (capped) cannula, the play specialist shows Noah what will happen and lets him 'do it' to the doll.
Noah chooses to sit on his dad's lap and play a tablet game. The procedure is done in the treatment room, not at his bed.
Afterwards Bea praises him, acknowledges it hurt a bit, and he draws a picture about it during post-procedural play.

teach.text: Do not confuse PREPARATION play (before: explain and rehearse with dolls and real equipment) with DISTRACTION (during: shift attention). And do not offer a false choice such as 'Shall we do your blood test now?' when it must happen.

items: Therapeutic play: diagnostic, preparation, distraction and post-procedural (debrief).
Prepare honestly, including about pain and what will help (NG204 1.6.2).
Match distraction to age and stage; let the child choose where choices are real.
Do painful procedures in the treatment room so the bed and play areas stay safe.
Believe and acknowledge pain; never minimise it.

summary: You can now prepare a child honestly for a procedure using play, choose distraction that fits their developmental stage, protect safe spaces on the ward, and support the child afterwards. You can also explain the role of the health play specialist.

A.q: Freya, 6, asks the nurse, 'Will my blood test hurt?' Which reply is most appropriate?
options: 'No, it won't hurt, I promise you.'
'Don't worry about that, let's talk about something else.'
'Brave girls don't cry, so you'll be fine.'
'It may pinch for a moment; the cream and a game will help.'
A.why: NG204 1.6.2: be honest about possible pain and what will be done to alleviate it. Honesty builds trust for future procedures.

whyNot.0: A false promise damages trust when it does hurt.
whyNot.1: Avoiding the question leaves her anxious and uninformed.
whyNot.2: This minimises her feelings and adds pressure not to show distress.

A.q: Aiden, 18 months, needs a nasogastric tube passed. No play specialist is available. Which distraction best suits his stage?
options: Guided imagery of a favourite place
Blowing bubbles for him to watch
A look-and-find book with small details
Counting backwards from 20 together
A.why: Toddlers have short attention spans and respond to simple, sensory distraction such as bubbles or noisy toys.

whyNot.0: Guided imagery needs language and imagination beyond an 18-month-old.
whyNot.2: Detailed look-and-find books suit older preschool and school-age children.
whyNot.3: Counting backwards is beyond a toddler's language and number skills.

A.q: Sienna, 5, needs a cannula. She is in a four-bed bay and the treatment room is free. Where should the procedure be done, and why?
options: The treatment room, so her bed stays a safe place
At her bed, as familiar surroundings calm her
In the play room, where she feels relaxed
At her bed, with curtains drawn for privacy
A.why: NG204 1.8.3: separate treatment areas from play and recreation, so the bed space and play areas remain safe spaces.

whyNot.1: Doing painful procedures at the bed can make the bed feel unsafe afterwards.
whyNot.2: Play areas should be kept free of treatment.
whyNot.3: Curtains give privacy but the bed space still becomes linked with pain.

B.q: A health play specialist uses a doll with a cannula and real, safe equipment to show Oscar, 4, what will happen tomorrow. Which type of therapeutic play is this?
options: Distraction play
Post-procedural play
Preparation play
Normalising play
B.why: Preparation play uses medically adapted dolls, role play and real equipment to explain and rehearse a procedure beforehand.

whyNot.0: Distraction is used during the procedure to shift attention.
whyNot.1: Post-procedural play happens afterwards to debrief.
whyNot.3: Normalising play is ordinary play that keeps life as usual on the ward.

B.q: Lily, 4, says she must have been naughty because she has to stay in hospital. What is the most helpful response?
options: Explain she is there to get better, not as a punishment
Tell her she will go home sooner if she behaves well
Reassure her that all children have to come to hospital
Change the subject to an activity she enjoys
B.why: Young children may interpret illness as punishment. A simple, honest explanation corrects the misunderstanding; diagnostic and preparation play can explore her fears further.

whyNot.1: Linking discharge to behaviour reinforces the idea that hospital is a punishment.
whyNot.2: This is untrue and does not address her belief.
whyNot.3: Distraction leaves her misunderstanding in place.

B.q: Daniel, 13, is due to have planned spinal surgery next month. Which preparation approach best suits his stage of development?
options: A picture book read to him the morning of surgery
Telling his parents and letting them decide what to share
Puppet play to show him what will happen
Detailed information, questions answered and a say in decisions
B.why: Adolescents value detailed, honest information, the chance to ask questions privately and involvement in decisions about their care (NG204).

whyNot.0: A picture book on the day suits a much younger child and gives no time to process.
whyNot.1: Young people should receive information directly and be involved in decisions.
whyNot.2: Puppet play suits preschool children rather than a 13-year-old.

C.q: Ruby, 4, is fighting and very distressed as the nurse prepares to take a routine blood sample for a non-urgent test. Her father offers to hold her down. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Proceed quickly with her father holding her firmly
Pause, calm Ruby and plan another attempt with preparation
Ask two more staff to help restrain her
Send the request back and cancel the test
C.why: For a non-urgent test, pausing allows calming, preparation and distraction, with play specialist support, rather than forcing a frightened child.

whyNot.0: Holding a distressed child down for a non-urgent test causes fear and harms trust in future procedures.
whyNot.2: Escalating restraint is not justified for a non-urgent test.
whyNot.3: The test is still needed; the aim is to do it in a way she can cope with.

C.q: After a painful dressing change, Jamal, 7, says it really hurt. A student nurse replies, 'That didn't really hurt, you're fine now.' How should the nurse respond?
options: Agree with the student to keep Jamal calm
Tell Jamal he will get a sticker if he stops crying
Ask Jamal's mother to explain it was not painful
Acknowledge his pain and review analgesia for next time
C.why: NG204 1.6.2: uphold children's experience of pain and avoid language that minimises it; pain should be assessed and acted on.

whyNot.0: Agreeing minimises his experience and undermines trust.
whyNot.1: A reward for not crying dismisses his pain.
whyNot.2: Asking his mother to deny his pain also minimises it.

C.q: Maya, 8, needs daily injections during her admission. Which plan best uses therapeutic play over the week?
options: Distraction on day 1, then no play once she is used to it
Play support once she becomes distressed
Preparation first, distraction during, then debrief play
Debrief play first, then preparation if she asks
C.why: Preparation before, distraction during and post-procedural (debrief) play after helps the child understand, cope and build strategies for future procedures.

whyNot.0: Repeated procedures still benefit from ongoing support; coping can change.
whyNot.1: Waiting for distress misses the chance to prevent it.
whyNot.3: Debrief comes after the procedure; preparation comes first.

reteach.title: Before, during, after
reteach.question: What does a frightened child need at each stage of a procedure?

blocks.body: BEFORE: understand what will happen (preparation play, honest words, pain relief). DURING: something else to focus on (distraction matched to age), a parent's comfort, a safe place. AFTER: a chance to talk or play it through, praise and belief in their pain.

blocks.text: 'It won't hurt' is a promise you cannot keep. 'It may pinch, and here is what will help' is honest.

explain.body: Diagnostic (what does the child understand?), preparation (explain and rehearse), distraction (during), post-procedural (debrief). Normalising play keeps everyday life going.

test.q: Which type of play gives a child the chance to work through what happened after a procedure?
options: Post-procedural play
Preparation play
Distraction play
Diagnostic play
test.why: Post-procedural play gives an opportunity to debrief and express feelings.

whyNot.2: Distraction is used during the procedure.
whyNot.3: Diagnostic play explores understanding and fears, usually beforehand.

explain.body: Explain what will happen, be honest about possible pain and what will help, use play and a calm environment, and do not minimise pain afterwards (NG204 1.6.2).

test.q: Which statement follows NICE NG204 on preparing a child for a painful procedure?
options: Avoid mentioning pain to prevent anxiety
Tell the child after it is over what was done
Be honest about possible pain and how it will be eased
Leave explanations to the parents at home
test.why: NG204 1.6.2 recommends honesty about possible pain and what will be done to alleviate it.

whyNot.0: Avoiding the topic leaves the child unprepared.
whyNot.1: Preparation should come before the procedure.
whyNot.3: Professionals should prepare the child directly, involving parents.

explain.body: Babies: holding, touch, feeding. Toddlers: bubbles, noisy toys. Preschool: stories, puppets. School age: games, I-spy, tablets. Teenagers: music, guided imagery, breathing.

test.q: Which distraction technique best suits a 15-year-old having a cannula?
options: A light-up rattle to shake
Music and focused breathing
Blowing bubbles to watch
A puppet show at the bedside
test.why: Teenagers often prefer music, guided imagery and breathing techniques that give them control.

whyNot.2: Bubbles suit toddlers and young children.

explain.body: Painful procedures happen in the treatment room, keeping the bed and play areas safe. Offer real choices (whose lap, which distraction) without implying the child can refuse a necessary procedure.

test.q: Which question offers a child a real choice before a necessary blood test?
options: Would you like to sit on Mum's lap or the chair?
Shall we do your blood test now or not today?
Do you want to have your blood test?
Can I do your blood test if you're good?
test.why: Choosing where to sit gives genuine control without implying the needed test is optional.

whyNot.1: This implies the test can be refused when it is needed.
whyNot.2: This offers a false choice about a necessary test.
whyNot.3: Linking the test to being 'good' is a false choice and adds pressure.
